text.p: Hilton Hotels Corp expects to report a fourth quarter 1996 loss in the high $0.30s per share range due largely to non-recurring charges and weakness in its high-stakes baccarat business, senior vice president Marc Grossman said.
He said the charges would total about $200 million, or nearly $0.60 a share, most of them arising from the company's $2 billion purchase of the Bally Entertainment Corp.
The baccarat losses would cut earnings by $0.10 to $0.12, Grossman said. "The end result is there's a loss (for the quarter) in the high 30 cents range," he said.
Hilton reported earnings of $0.32 a share in the fourth quarter of 1995.

Grossman said Arthur Goldberg, the new head of the company's gambling division, would take a close look at the baccarat business "not with the idea of getting out of it, but just looking at our policies, our procedures to make sure we're in it in a way that is going to be profitable for us."
He said big-stakes baccarat is a "very, very volatile business" because the results can be determined by the luck of a handful of high-rollers.

"It's a small universe, but you're talking about people who come in over the course of a weekend and will wager $5 million, $10 million, $15 million. You can see where the swings come in," Grossman said.
"It really boils down to a matter of luck. We have not played lucky," he said.

Grossman would not discuss the outlook for the first quarter of 1997, but said the addition of the Bally properties and rising room rates in the Hilton hotel properties gave the company hope that the year would be a good one.
"We're looking forward to what we think will be a good year," he said. The Bally casinos in Las Vegas and Atlantic City performed "extremely well" in 1996 and should do so again this year, he said.

Also, Grossman said, "we believe the full-service hotel business is going to continue to go gang-busters." He said said rising demand and a supply that has not expanded since the late 1980s were boosting room rates and profits.
"We're able to drive room rates," he said. "For every dollar you raise rates, about 90 cents goes to the bottom line."
